Scottish Police Forcibly Drug Tested over 100 People Waiting in Line to Enter Dance Club

Hundreds of clubbers in Scotland got a shock last weekend when police with sniffer dogs swooped on a nightclub queue and demanded to drug test them before entry.

As customers waited to enter Club Tropicana in Aberdeen, officers with dogs and a CCTV van stood at the club’s entrance and insisted on swabbing the hands of over 100 people.

According to Scotland’s Daily Record, those who wouldn’t co-operate were to be refused entry while those testing positive faced being questioned, searched, and arrested.

CCTV monitored the process as the palms of partygoers were swabbed for traces of illegal drugs including cannabis, ecstasy, cocaine, and heroin.

The industrial scale search was carried out using the Itemiser, a £25,000 portable testing device designed to indicate if someone has handled drugs by reading a swab taken from their hands.

Club boss Tony Cochrane said he was given an hour’s notice that the controversial procedure would be taking place on his doorstep. “I ­support an anti-drug policy but I feel this latest action by Police Scotland is a step too far in regards to civil ­liberties,” he told the Daily Record, adding that the police found nothing despite attending the nightspot on Friday and Saturday nights.

The heavy-handed tactics by Police Scotland were rapidly criticised by politicians who demanded the force review their techniques and explain how the use of mass “stop-and-swab” measures help address drug taking.

“Where police spring tests upon people and there’s a ­pressure to co-operate, it adds ­concern about the giving of consent and whether operations like this are appropriate,” Labour justice spokesman Graeme Pearson told the Daily Record.

Responding to the criticism, Police Scotland said: “These operations are carried out regularly across the city centre’s licensed premises as part of Police Scotland’s duty to keep people safe. They are set up in advance and done with the full co-operation of the premises’ managers and staff.”

The highly dubious use of manpower and resources to make citizens feel like suspects happened after revelations that Scotland’s stop-and-search figures are highest in the U.K., leaving people concerned that officers are driven by meeting targets rather than fighting crime.
